date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: The unsolved-murder rite is prescribed in Deut 21:1–9: a man found slain in the field, murderer unknown; the nearest city's elders perform the rite.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 21:1–9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); zero diffs in the KJV check.

claims.claim: The nearest city is determined by measurement by the elders and judges (21:2).
claims.evidence: JFB (Sanhedrin deputation per Jewish writers); K&D.

claims.claim: The heifer has never been worked or yoked; its neck is broken in a rough, uncultivated valley with constantly flowing water (21:3–4).
claims.evidence: K&D (valley with water constantly flowing).

claims.claim: The rite is NOT a sacrifice: no slaughtering, no sprinkling of blood, no altar; the neck-breaking is a symbolic execution of the unknown murderer.
claims.evidence: K&D; Milgrom (heifer need not be unblemished, Sot. 9:5 — rabbinic source cited second-hand).

claims.claim: The priests, the sons of Levi, are present as witnesses/representatives to receive and acknowledge the declaration, not as officiants conducting a sacrifice.
The elders wash their hands over the heifer, declare "Our hands have not shed this blood", and pray for atonement, "that the blood shall not be imputed unto them" (21:6–9).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 21:6–9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: If the murderer is later found, he still dies; the rite does not pardon a known murderer.
claims.evidence: K&D; Milgrom, citing Sot. 9:7 — the Talmud was not read directly; second-hand via Milgrom.

claims.claim: Blood shed on the ground pollutes the land; the rite addresses that pollution (cf. Num 35:33).
claims.evidence: Milgrom (Num 35:33; Gen 4:11–12; 2 Sam 21:1 LXX; Ezek 22:24); JFB (expiation of bloodguilt).

claims.claim: A Hittite parallel exists: Hittite Code §6 — a corpse found in open country is interred on the spot and the owner loses his rights to the area; the rite's purpose is the transfer of pollution from desirable to undesirable land.
claims.evidence: Milgrom, citing Hittite Code §6 via Pritchard, *ANET* p. 189 — the Hittite text was not read directly; second-hand via Milgrom.

claims.claim: LH §§23–24 address the same problem (unsolved robbery/murder) with money: the city and governor restore the property and pay one mina of silver for a life lost — the opposite remedy to Deut 21:1–9.
claims.evidence: Code of Hammurabi §§23–24, Johns translation, read directly.

claims.claim: The captive-wife law is prescribed in Deut 21:10–14: a beautiful captive taken in war may be married after a month of mourning.
claims.evidence: JFB; K&D.

claims.claim: The month of mourning, shaving of the head, paring of the nails and laying aside of the garments of captivity are signs of purification and of transition from her people (cf. Ps 45:11).
claims.evidence: K&D (purification signs; month to forget her people); JFB (war custom "improved" by Moses).

claims.claim: If the husband has "no delight in her", she goes free where she will; she shall not be sold for money or treated as merchandise (21:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 21:14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The law applies to wars with surrounding nations after the conquest, not to Canaanites (Deut 7:3).
claims.evidence: K&D, citing Deut 7:3.

claims.claim: The true firstborn receives a double portion ("a mouth of two"), protected against the father's preference for the son of the beloved wife (21:15–17).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 21:15–17, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D.

claims.claim: "Beloved" and "hated" (21:15): JFB read the two wives as successive marriages (the first dead) with "no bearing upon polygamy"; K&D read them as two wives, one loved and one less loved.
claims.evidence: JFB vs K&D, both read in full.

claims.claim: Primogeniture predates Moses; the law secures the firstborn's right rather than originating it.
claims.evidence: K&D (hereditary tradition; pre-Mosaic).

claims.claim: The rebellious-son procedure is prescribed in Deut 21:18–21: stubborn, rebellious, glutton and drunkard; both parents bring him to the elders at the gate; the men of the city stone him.
claims.evidence: JFB; K&D.

claims.claim: Both parents' consent is required and the elders at the gate decide; the parents lose the right to kill the son themselves — the charge itself, brought by both parents before the magistrates, is the proof.
claims.evidence: K&D (charge as proof; Schnell); JFB (both parents' consent as safeguard).

claims.claim: No narrative in the Hebrew Bible records the execution of a rebellious son under Deut 21:18–21.
claims.evidence: Absence claim (no narrative instance found); the rabbinic tradition that it was never carried out (m. Sanhedrin 8:4) was not read directly.

claims.claim: Hanging (21:22–23) is post-execution display (gibbeting after death by the sword, cf. Num 25:4), not the method of execution; the body must be buried the same day.
claims.evidence: K&D (hanging after execution; Josh 8:29; 10:26–27); JFB (gibbeting after execution).

claims.claim: "He that is hanged is accursed of God" (21:23); exposure defiles the land.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 21:23, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D (land defiled by exposure, not decomposition).

claims.claim: The hanging-and-burial rule is applied in narrative: Josh 8:29 (king of Ai) and Josh 10:26–27.
claims.evidence: Josh 8:29; 10:26–27, cited by K&D and verified against the live API verse counts (Josh 8:35; 10:43).

claims.claim: Lost property and neighbour duties are prescribed in Deut 22:1–4: return the stray ox, sheep, ass or garment; keep it until the owner seeks it; help lift a fallen animal. "Brother" means any human being, including an enemy.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 22:1–4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB; K&D (cf. Ex 23:4).

claims.claim: LH §§9–13 address lost property with a capital procedure: the loser proves ownership before witnesses; the seller who cannot produce the vendor is a thief and is put to death; the buyer loses his money — the opposite of Deut 22:1–4.
claims.evidence: Code of Hammurabi §§9–13, Johns translation, read directly.

claims.claim: Ex 23:4–5 extends the duty to an enemy's straying animal and fallen ass.
claims.evidence: K&D, citing Ex 23:4–5.

claims.claim: Deut 22:5 prohibits wearing the garments of the opposite sex. The rationale is disputed: K&D ground it in the creation-order distinction of the sexes; JFB attribute it to disguises used in heathen temples. The text states no rationale.
claims.evidence: K&D vs JFB.

claims.claim: The bird's-nest law (22:6–7): take the young, not the dam; the same promise of long life as the parental commandment (Deut 5:16 / Ex 20:12). The rationale is humane and preservative.
claims.evidence: JFB (humanising spirit; Michaelis on birds and pests); K&D (parental affection).

claims.claim: The parapet (22:8) presupposes flat roofs in use as living space.
claims.evidence: JFB; K&D.

claims.claim: The mixtures (22:9–11) — mixed seed, mixed yoking of ox and ass, wool and linen together — repeat Lev 19:19.
claims.evidence: Lev 19:19 (verse counts verified: Lev 19:37).

claims.claim: No rationale for the mixture prohibitions is stated in the text; proposed explanations (separation of kinds, Canaanite practice, symbolic holiness) were not verified from a primary scholarly source read directly.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 22:9–11, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); no directly-read source establishes a rationale.

claims.claim: Fringes on the four quarters of the vesture (22:12) restate the tassel ordinance of Num 15:37–41; JFB note these are "not the same as Nu 15:38", i.e. a briefer restatement.
claims.evidence: Num 15:37–41 (verified: Num 15:41); JFB.

claims.claim: The virginity-slander case is prescribed in Deut 22:13–21: a husband who hates his bride and charges her with not being a virgin brings the case before the elders at the gate.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 22:13–21, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The "tokens of virginity" (22:15, 17) are the marks on the bed-clothes produced before the elders.
claims.evidence: K&D.

claims.claim: A false accuser is chastised, fined 100 shekels of silver (double the seducer's 50 in v. 29), and loses the right of divorce for ever (22:18–19).
claims.evidence: K&D (100 = double the 50).

claims.claim: A true charge means stoning at the door of her father's house (22:20–21).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 22:20–21, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Adultery (22:22): both the man and the woman die. LH §129 agrees on death for both but drowns them and allows the husband or the king to pardon — a pardon clause Deuteronomy lacks.
claims.evidence: LH §129, Johns translation, read directly.

claims.claim: The betrothed virgin in the city (22:23–24): both die — she because she cried not, being in the city; he because he humbled his neighbour's wife. A betrothed woman is treated as a wife.
claims.evidence: K&D (betrothed = wife).

claims.claim: The betrothed virgin in the field (22:25–27): the man only dies; the woman is free — the case is likened to murder, "for as when a man riseth against his neighbour, and slayeth him, even so is this matter".
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 22:25–27, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D ("no death-sin" in the woman).

claims.claim: The unbetrothed virgin (22:28–29): fifty shekels of silver, marriage, and no divorce ever. The parallel in Ex 22:16–17 states the father's right of refusal, which Deuteronomy omits here.
claims.evidence: Ex 22:16–17 (verified: Ex 22:31); K&D.

claims.claim: "Lay hold on her" (22:28): whether the act is force or seduction is disputed — K&D treat it as seizure; Ex 22:16 uses "entice".
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 22:28, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (for the quoted wording 'Lay hold on her'); Ex 22:16; K&D.

claims.claim: A man shall not take his father's wife (22:30); the parallel is Lev 18:7–8. K&D read v. 30 as the close of the chastity laws rather than the opening of ch 23.
claims.evidence: Lev 18:7–8 (verified: Lev 18:30); K&D.

claims.claim: Exclusions from the congregation of the LORD are prescribed in Deut 23:1–8: the wounded/eunuch, the *mamzer* to the tenth generation, the Ammonite and the Moabite for ever, the Edomite and the Egyptian in the third generation.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 23:1–8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: *Mamzer* (23:2): K&D follow the Talmud and the Rabbins — a child begotten in incest or adultery, etymology obscure, only other occurrence Zech 9:6; JFB treat it more broadly as illegitimate birth.
claims.evidence: K&D; JFB. The Talmud was not read directly.

claims.claim: The Ammonite/Moabite exclusion is explained in the text itself: inhospitality (no bread and water on the way) and hiring Balaam to curse Israel (23:4–5), not their incestuous origin.
claims.evidence: K&D.

claims.claim: The Edomite ("he is thy brother") and the Egyptian ("thou wast a stranger in his land") are admissible in the third generation (great-grandchildren), by incorporation through circumcision.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 23:7–8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D.

claims.claim: Camp purity is prescribed in Deut 23:9–14: cleanliness in war, the latrine outside the camp, "for the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee".
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 23:9–14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The fugitive servant (23:15–16) shall not be returned to his master; he shall dwell where he chooses and shall not be oppressed. This directly reverses LH §§16–20 (death for harbouring; two shekels' reward for return) and contrasts with Greek and Roman practice, where fugitives were returned or sheltered only in temples.
claims.evidence: LH §§16–20, Johns translation, read directly; JFB citing Xenophon, Florus and Michaelis — second-hand via JFB.

claims.claim: Cult prostitution is forbidden in Deut 23:17–18: no *qedeshah* or *qedesh* among Israel; "the hire of a whore, or the price of a dog" shall not be brought into the house of the LORD. "Price of a dog" is the gains of the male *kadesh*, not the sale price of a dog.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 23:17–18, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D (*qedesh/qedeshah* = Astarte prostitution, Gen 38:21).

claims.claim: Usury (23:19–20): no interest from a brother (countryman); interest permitted from a stranger. The rationale offered is that a simple society needs no interest, while foreign trade does.
Vows (23:21–23): pay what you vow; it is no sin not to vow; the parallel is Num 30:2.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 23:21–23, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Num 30:2 (verified: Num 30:16).

claims.claim: A neighbour's vineyard and corn (23:24–25): eat your fill by hand, but put no sickle to your neighbour's standing corn; the practice was still recognised among Arabs in K&D's day.
claims.evidence: K&D.

claims.claim: Deut 24:1–4: divorce is assumed as custom and regulated, not instituted as a right. Vv. 1–3 are the protasis (a bill of divorcement is written; she marries another) and v. 4 the apodosis (the former husband may not take her again "after that she is defiled").
claims.evidence: K&D (protasis/apodosis); JFB (divorce tolerated, Mt 19:8).

claims.claim: *Ervat davar* ("some uncleanness", 24:1) is disputed: the school of Shammai read it strictly, the school of Hillel widely ("for every cause", Matt 19:3). Adultery is excluded, since it carried the death penalty.
claims.evidence: K&D.

claims.claim: The newly married man is free from war and public business for a year, "that he may cheer up his wife" (24:5).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 24:5, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB (exemption favouring matrimony).

claims.claim: The millstone pledge (24:6): "No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge" — the handmill ground the household's daily bread.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 24:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB (handmill, daily grinding); K&D (mill as specimen, like clothing in Ex 22:25–26).

claims.claim: Man-stealing (24:7) is a capital offence; the parallel is Ex 21:16, and LH §14 agrees (death for stealing a freeman's son).
claims.evidence: Ex 21:16 (verified: Ex 21:36); LH §14, Johns translation, read directly.

claims.claim: Leprosy (24:8–9): "Take heed in the plague of leprosy… remember what the LORD thy God did unto Miriam" — a warning against the plague, not instruction in diagnosis.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 24:8–9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D.

claims.claim: Pledge procedure (24:10–13): the lender stays outside the house; the poor man's garment is returned by sunset — "it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God" (cf. Deut 6:25). The parallel is Ex 22:26–27.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 24:10–13, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Ex 22:26–27 (verified: Ex 22:31); K&D.

claims.claim: The day labourer's wage (24:14–15) is paid the same day, before the sun goes down, "for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it" (cf. Lev 19:13; Jas 5:4). LH §273 fixes a daily wage (six gerahs to the fifth month, five after) — a fixed rate, where Deuteronomy stresses timing and need.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 24:14–15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Lev 19:13 (verified: Lev 19:37); LH §273, Johns translation, read directly.

claims.claim: Individual responsibility (24:16): "The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin" — addressed to the magistrates, against the heathen practice of killing criminals' families.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 24:16, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D (Persians, Macedonians; Esth 9:13–14; Herod. iii.19).

claims.claim: Justice for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (24:17–18) is grounded in the Exodus memory: "thou wast a bondman in Egypt" (cf. Ex 22:20–21; 23:9).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 24:17–18, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Gleanings (24:19–22): the forgotten sheaf, the beaten olive tree and the gleaned vineyard are for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (cf. Lev 19:9–10; 23:22).
claims.evidence: Lev 19:9–10 (verified: Lev 19:37); K&D.

claims.claim: Forty stripes maximum (25:1–3): the judge causes the beating in his presence, "forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed", lest the brother seem vile. LH §202 prescribes sixty stripes with a cow-hide whip for striking a superior. The rabbis later fixed forty save one (2 Cor 11:24).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 25:1–3, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); LH §202, Johns translation, read directly; K&D (Egyptian whipping on monuments, Wilkinson and Rosellini).

claims.claim: "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn" (25:4). The command is "proverbial" in nature; Paul applies it generally to the labourer's wages (1 Cor 9:9; 1 Tim 5:18).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 25:4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D; 1 Cor 9:9; 1 Tim 5:18 (verse counts verified).

claims.claim: The levirate duty (25:5–6): brothers dwelling together; one dies childless; the widow shall not marry outside the family; her brother-in-law shall take her, and the firstborn "shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel". *Yabam* (H2992) is a denominative Pi'el verb, "do the duty of *yabam* to a brother's widow".
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 25:5–6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); BDB H2992, read via the BibleHub lexicon page (Deut 25:5 perfect consecutive; Gen 38:8 imperative; Deut 25:7 infinitive suffix).

claims.claim: The levirate predates Moses: Gen 38:8 (Onan and Tamar) is the pre-Mosaic instance.
claims.evidence: K&D; JFB; Gen 38:8 (verse count verified: Gen 38:30).

claims.claim: The refusal rite (25:7–10, *halitzah*): the widow looses his shoe and spits in his face before the elders; his house is called "the house of him that hath his shoe loosed". The shoe-loosing is the renunciation of position and property (cf. Ruth 4:7); whether the spitting is in the face (K&D) or on the ground (the Talmudists) is disputed.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 25:7–10, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D; the Talmud was not read directly.

claims.claim: Ruth 4:7 applies the shoe rite to redemption and exchange by a *go'el*, not to levirate marriage proper; Ruth 4 is redemption, not a levirate marriage under Deut 25:5–10.
claims.evidence: K&D (Ruth 4:7); JFB (obligation extends to the nearest kinsman, Ruth 4:4).

claims.claim: The immodest woman (25:11–12): the hand is cut off. K&D (following Baumgarten) read this as added lest the widow's independence in the levirate procedure be read as female licence.
claims.evidence: K&D.

claims.claim: Weights and measures (25:13–16): "Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small… a perfect and just weight shalt thou have" — "a stone and a stone" in the Hebrew, large for buying and small for selling (cf. Lev 19:35–36).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 25:13–16, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Lev 19:35–36 (verified: Lev 19:37); K&D.

claims.claim: Archaeology: hundreds of inscribed stone weights from Iron Age Judah have been recovered, many deviating from standard; a 2021 City of David limestone weight (marked two gerah, weighing 3.61 g) was reported as a possible "cheater's weight", but the reading is disputed (Hendin: eight gerah, ~3.84–4.56 g). It is not settled evidence of fraud.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining.org, "Weights and Measures", read in part (lines 0–160 of 415); the 2021 find via BAR/CoinWeek search snippets only — second-hand, not read in full.

claims.claim: Amalek (25:17–19): "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt; how he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God." The attack on the stragglers is Deuteronomy's addition to the Rephidim narrative (Ex 17:8–16).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 25:17–18, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Ex 17:8–16 (verified: Ex 17:16); K&D (*zanav*, cf. Josh 10:19).

claims.claim: The Amalek command (25:19) is conditional on rest in the land and commands that the remembrance of Amalek be blotted out from under heaven, with "thou shalt not forget". It is presented as stated; it is not neutralised by asserting hyperbole.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 25:19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (for the quoted wording 'thou shalt not forget'); Phase 2 Correction Record (herem rule).

claims.claim: No narrative in the Hebrew Bible records the heifer rite (21:1–9) being performed.
claims.evidence: Absence claim (no narrative instance found).

claims.claim: No narrative records a levirate marriage contracted as the statute of Deut 25:5–10; Gen 38 is pre-Mosaic custom and Ruth 4 is redemption by a *go'el*. The Amalek command is attempted in 1 Sam 15, and Amalekites still appear afterwards (1 Sam 27:8; 30:1–18; 2 Sam 8:12; 1 Chr 4:43), so a completed blotting-out is not attested.
claims.evidence: Absence claim; 1 Sam 15:1–3 (verified: 1 Sam 15:35); 1 Sam 30:1–18 (verified: 1 Sam 30:31).

claims.claim: No independently established historical date exists for this category (Standards §3.1). The text's own frame is Moses' address on the plains of Moab (Deut 1:5); that is the text's claim, not an established historical date.
claims.evidence: Standards v1.1 §3.1.

claims.claim: None of the eight documented errors in the Phase 2 Correction Record touches Category 6 directly (they fall in categories 7, 9, 3/5, 1/7/10, 4, and source integrity generally).
claims.evidence: `DEUTERONOMY-PHASE2-FINAL-REPORT.md`.

claims.claim: The block is arranged as case law by example, not as a systematic code; ch 22 is a set of examples showing "love should rule" in neighbourly life.
claims.evidence: K&D (ch 22 introduction; ch 21 grouping).

connections.note: Blood pollutes the land; the rite addresses bloodguilt.
Priests decide hard cases; the heifer rite puts priests present as witnesses.
Captives taken in war; the captive-wife law regulates one case.
Reuben, "my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength".
Striking or cursing a parent is a capital offence; the rebellious-son procedure is the judicial form.
"Chasten thy son while there is hope" — wisdom on discipline, not the judicial procedure.
The king of Ai is hanged and buried the same day — the rule applied.
The five kings are hanged and buried the same day.
Paul quotes "Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree".
Bodies not to remain on the cross on the Sabbath day.
The enemy's straying ox or ass; the fallen ass — the same duty, extended to an enemy.
"Whether it be cow or ewe, ye shall not kill it and her young both in one day" — the same sparing of mother and young.
Mixtures: seed, cattle, cloth — the fuller form of the prohibition.
Fringes/tassels with a ribband of blue.
"The adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death".
The woman taken in adultery; note the pericope's textual status (absent from the earliest manuscripts).
Mary is betrothed to Joseph; he is "minded to put her away privily" — betrothal treated as marriage.
The seduced virgin: dowry, marriage, and the father's right of refusal.
"The nakedness of thy father… thou shalt not uncover".
"That one should have his father's wife".
The eunuch is not cut off: "neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree" — prophetic development of the exclusion.
The exclusion is read in Nehemiah's day and the Ammonite and Moabite are separated from Israel.
Ruth the Moabitess is taken as wife; the tension with the exclusion is noted, not resolved.
Balak sends for Balaam to curse Israel — the narrative behind the exclusion.
"Meddle not with [Edom]: for I will not give you of their land" — Edom is thy brother.
"There were also sodomites in the land" — the practice the law forbids, attested in the monarchy.
"If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer".
"Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury, nor lend him thy victuals for increase".
"If a man vow a vow unto the LORD… he shall not break his word".
"When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it".
The disciples pluck the ears of corn — the law in practice.
The same event as Matt 12:1.
The same event as Matt 12:1.
"They say, If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man's, shall he return unto her again?" — the divorce law cited.
"Whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery".
"Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives".
The same teaching as Matt 19:3–9.
"Whosoever putteth away his wife, and marrieth another, committeth adultery".
The newly betrothed man is exempt from war — the same concern for the new marriage.
The pledged garment returned by sunset — the same protection of the poor man's necessities.
"He that stealeth a man, and selleth him… shall surely be put to death".
Miriam becomes leprous — the event the law cites as a warning.
The pledge procedure: the lender stays outside; the garment is returned by sunset.
"The wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning".
"The hire of the labourers… which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth".
Amaziah "slew not the children of the murderers: according to that which is written in the book of the law of Moses" — the rule applied.
"Every one shall die for his own iniquity" — the prophetic development of individual responsibility.
"The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father".
Tension noted, not resolved: God's "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children" is divine visitation, not a judicial rule for magistrates.
"Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child".
"Thou shalt not oppress a stranger: for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt".
Gleanings for the poor and the stranger.
Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz — the gleaning law in narrative.
"Of the Jews five times received I forty stripes save one".
Paul quotes "Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn".
Paul quotes the same verse for the labourer's wages.
Judah commands Onan: "Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother" — the pre-Mosaic instance.
The kinsman-redeemer at the gate; the shoe rite is used — but this is redemption by a *go'el*, not levirate marriage proper (clm-deu-06-069).
The Sadducees cite Moses: "If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife".
The same citation as Matt 22:24.
The same citation as Matt 22:24.
"Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure… just balances, just weights".
"A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight".
"Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD".
"Making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit".
"Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?"
Amalek fights Israel at Rephidim; Moses' hands are held up; the LORD swears war with Amalek.
Samuel's command to Saul: "smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have" — the attempted execution of the command.
The Amalekites raid Ziklag; David defeats them — Amalekites still present after Saul.
Haman "the Agagite" — the book's own identification; the descent from Agag is the book's claim, not an independently established genealogy.
